intro: A novel is the longest thing most people ever read on purpose. Two hundred pages, sometimes five hundred, about people who never existed, doing things that never happened. And yet readers cry over them, argue about them, and remember them for the rest of their lives. Something is going on in those pages that a summary cannot give you, and this unit is about learning to see it.

You will take a novel apart the way a mechanic takes apart an engine, not to ruin it but to understand why it runs. You will learn how writers build a character out of nothing but words, how they make a person change across a whole book, and who gets to tell the story and why that matters. You will learn the shape of a plot, what a setting is for, and the difference between what a story is about and what it says. You will learn to spot a symbol and to prove it is one.

Then you will learn to read a whole book on your own: with stamina, a pencil, a journal, and the right questions. You will read three short masters closely, learn the rules of five kinds of story, give a book talk, and pick your next book wisely. The novel this site keeps its own room for, The Outsiders, will be the example again and again. But every tool here works on any book with a person in it.
bigQuestion: How does a made-up story about particular people become something true that a reader carries for life?

the reason a character does what they do
a character who changes in an important inner way during the story

the turning point of highest tension in a plot

test.q: 'Nobody at the table could remember Grandpa ever raising his voice.' This reveals character through:
choices: How others react to the character
test.why: The evidence is other people's experience of him, one of the five kinds of indirect characterization.

test.q: Which best defines a character's motivation?
choices: The trait stated by the narrator
The reason behind the character's actions
test.why: Motivation is the want or fear that drives what a character does.

test.q: A best friend who is loyal from the first page to the last is:
test.why: A character whose inner self does not change is static, however admirable.

test.q: A girl wants to move away for college but cannot bear to leave her grandmother. This conflict is:
test.why: The struggle is inside one person between two things she wants.

test.q: A narrator uses 'he' and reports only one character's thoughts. The point of view is:
test.why: Third person with access to only one mind is limited.

test.q: What is the strongest sign that a narrator is unreliable?
choices: Other characters' actions contradict the narrator's claims
test.why: A gap between the narrator's version and the evidence in the text signals unreliability.

test.q: Which is the strongest textual evidence that a character is brave?
choices: The narrator says she seems brave
On page 80 she goes back into the burning church for the children
test.why: A specific, checkable action from the text is the strongest evidence.

test.q: Which part of a plot introduces characters and the normal situation?
test.why: Exposition sets up who, where, and what is normal.

test.q: A character mentions early that the old bridge is unsafe; much later someone crosses it. This is:
test.why: An early hint that pays off later is foreshadowing.

test.q: Which statement is a theme rather than a topic or a moral?
choices: People divided by class often share the same fears
test.why: A theme is a full-sentence insight about life that does not depend on the characters' names.

test.q: In The Outsiders, why can the sunset be called a symbol?
choices: Because it repeats at key moments and characters treat it as meaning something shared
test.why: Repetition, placement, and characters' attention are the evidence that make an object a symbol.

test.q: What is the fairest way to compare a novel and its film?
choices: Pick one shared scene and argue which version serves the theme better
Decide which one is more fun
Assume the book is always better
test.why: A focused, evidence-based comparison treats each change as a choice with effects.

test.q: What are the three parts of a useful reading journal entry?
test.why: An entry records what you noticed, a question, and a prediction to check later.

test.q: In 'The Story of an Hour,' the doctors believe Mrs. Mallard died of joy, but the reader knows otherwise. This is:
test.why: Irony is the gap between what a character believes and what the reader understands.

test.q: A book has about four unknown words on a typical page. According to the page test, it is:
choices: A good stretch book to read with support
test.why: Three to five unknown words per page is the zone where a book stretches a reader without overwhelming.

write.prompt: Is Ponyboy Curtis a dynamic character, or does he end The Outsiders as the same boy who walked out of the theater? Take a side and support it with evidence from the beginning, a turning point, and the end of the novel.
tips: State your claim in one sentence: dynamic or static, and in what way.
Use at least three pieces of textual evidence: one from the first chapters, one from a turning point, one from the ending, with page numbers.
For each piece of evidence, write the reasoning that connects it to your claim; do not let quotes stand alone.
Name the strongest point the other side could make, such as the fact that Ponyboy still fights at the rumble, and answer it.
Finish by stating what the change, or the lack of change, says about the book's theme.

title: The Novel

chapters.title: Characters and Conflict
chapters.bigQuestion: How does a writer make a made-up person feel so real that you argue about what they should have done?

story.title: The Boy Outside the Theater
story.kicker: A novel written by a teenager opens with one boy, one sidewalk, and a feeling every reader knows.
paragraphs: The book opens with a boy stepping out of a movie theater into bright sunlight. He is alone, and he is thinking about two things: the actor Paul Newman, and how to get home. He has a long walk ahead of him, and he knows that a boy like him, walking alone in his part of town, might get jumped. He walks anyway. Within a few pages he is on the ground with a knife at his throat, and his older brothers are running to pull the attackers off.

The boy is Ponyboy Curtis, fourteen years old, the narrator of The Outsiders. The author, S. E. Hinton, started the novel when she was a high school student in Oklahoma and published it in 1967. She was tired of books about teenagers that did not sound like anyone she knew. So she wrote about the two groups at her own school: the greasers, poor kids with long, oiled hair, and the Socs, rich kids with nice cars. In her book, the greasers tell the story.

What makes that first scene work is not the fight. It is everything Ponyboy tells you before the fight. He says he likes movies and books, which most of his friends do not. He says his oldest brother, Darry, is hard on him. He says he wishes he looked tougher than he does. By the time the Socs pull up, you already know him. You are scared for him because you know him.

That is the trick of every good novel. A writer cannot hand you a real person. A writer can only hand you words: what a character says, does, wants, fears, and notices. From those words you build a person in your head. And once you have built him, you cannot help caring what happens to him. You will argue with friends about whether Darry loves Ponyboy or just bosses him. You will decide who is to blame for what happens in the park.

This chapter is about how that building happens. You will learn how writers show character, what pushes a character to act, how a person can change across three hundred pages, and who gets to tell the story. The Outsiders is the novel this site has its own room for, so it will come up often. But the tools work on any book with a person in it, which is nearly all of them.
story.think: Think of a character from a book, movie, or show you felt you knew. What did the writer show you first that made you care?

lessons.title: Telling and Showing
lessons.mainIdea: Writers reveal character two ways: by telling you directly, or by showing actions, words, looks and thoughts and letting you decide.
reading: Read these two sentences about the same girl. One: Maya was generous. Two: Maya slid half her sandwich across the table without looking up, as if she had never wanted the whole thing. The first sentence tells you what to think. The second makes you figure it out. Both are ways of building a character, and good writers use both.

When the narrator states a trait outright, that is *direct characterization*. It is fast and clear: "Darry was tough, cool, and smart." You do not have to guess. Writers use it when they need you to know something quickly, or when a narrator is the kind of person who sums people up.

When you have to infer a trait from evidence, that is *indirect characterization*. The evidence comes in five kinds: what the character says, what the character does, what the character thinks, how the character looks, and how other people react to the character. Maya sliding the sandwich is an action. Her not looking up is a small action that shows she does not want thanks.

Indirect characterization asks more of you, but it pays more back. When you work out that Maya is generous, you believe it, because you saw the proof. When a book tells you a character is brave and then never shows it, you stop trusting the book. Watch for the gap between what a narrator says about a person and what that person actually does.

words.d: when the narrator or another character states a trait outright, such as "he was stubborn"
when the reader infers a trait from a character's speech, actions, thoughts, looks, or how others treat them
a quality of a person's character, such as honesty, impatience, or courage

look.title: One Sentence, Two Methods
look.text: Mr. Ortiz was the most patient man on the block. He had explained the same bus schedule to Mrs. Kim four times that week, and on the fifth time he only smiled and pulled out a pencil.
look.prompt: Which sentence is direct characterization and which is indirect? Which one would convince you more if it stood alone?

check.q: Which of these is direct characterization?
choices: Lena slammed the door so hard the picture fell.
Everyone stepped back when Lena walked in.
Lena's jaw was tight and her fists were closed.
check.why: Only the second sentence states the trait outright. The others give evidence and let you infer it.

check.q: Which of the five kinds of indirect evidence is 'other people stepped back when she walked in'?
choices: How others react to the character
check.why: The evidence is other people's reaction, one of the five kinds of indirect characterization.

check.q: Why can indirect characterization be more convincing than direct?
choices: The reader sees the proof and draws the conclusion
Narrators are not allowed to state traits
check.why: When readers reach a conclusion from evidence, they believe it more than when they are simply told.

lessons.title: What a Character Wants
lessons.mainIdea: Motivation is the reason behind a character's actions, and finding it explains choices that look strange from outside.
reading: A boy in a novel steals a loaf of bread. Is he a thief? Then you read that his sister has not eaten in two days. Now the same act means something different. Nothing about the action changed. What changed is that you learned his *motivation*, the reason behind what he did.

Every character who matters wants something. It can be big, like freedom or revenge, or small, like being left alone for one afternoon. Writers rarely announce it. They let you see the character reach for it again and again. Ponyboy in The Outsiders wants to be seen as more than a greaser. That want explains why he keeps reading books and watching sunsets, even when his friends tease him.

To find motivation, ask two questions about any action: what does this character get from doing it, and what would they lose by not doing it? A character who lies to a friend might be protecting himself, protecting the friend, or protecting a secret. Each answer makes a different person.

Motivation is also where real conflict starts. Two characters who want different things will collide. Two characters who want the same thing, like one job or one parent's approval, will collide harder. When you can name what each person wants, the whole plot starts to make sense.

words.d: the reason a character does what they do, whether stated or hidden
to work out something not stated directly, using clues and what you already know

look.title: The Same Act, Three Reasons
look.text: Devon volunteers to stay after school and clean the art room every Friday. His teacher thinks he loves art. His best friend thinks he is avoiding the bus. His mother thinks he is hiding from his chores. Only one of them is right, and Devon is not saying.
look.prompt: What clue in a later chapter would prove each explanation right or wrong? Which clue would you look for first?

check.q: What is a character's motivation?
choices: The trait the narrator states most often
The reason behind what the character does
The problem the character faces at the end
check.why: Motivation is the why behind an action, the want or fear that drives it.

check.q: Learning that the boy's sister was hungry changed what about the bread scene?
check.why: The action was the same. The motivation changed how readers understand it.

check.q: Which situation would most likely create the strongest conflict?
choices: Two characters who want different things in different towns
Two characters who want nothing in particular
One character who gets everything easily
Two characters who want the same single thing
check.why: When two people want the same one thing, only one can have it, so they collide hardest.

lessons.title: Hearing Character in Dialogue
lessons.mainIdea: How a character talks, including word choice, what they avoid saying, and how they treat others, reveals who they are.
reading: Two brothers answer the same question: "Where were you?" The first says, "Out." The second says, "I went by the library, then I stopped at Marco's, and then I lost track of time, I'm sorry." You have never met these brothers. You already know that one is closed and one is open, one is maybe angry and one is anxious to be forgiven. Dialogue did that in twenty words.

*Dialogue* is the words characters speak. Writers use it to reveal character in several ways. Word choice shows education, region, and mood. Length shows whether a person is guarded or eager. What a character refuses to talk about can matter more than what they say. And how a character speaks to different people, gently to a child and sharply to a waiter, shows their values.

In The Outsiders, the greasers' slang marks them as a group, and it separates them from the Socs. But within the group, each boy sounds different. Two-Bit jokes constantly. Johnny says little, and when he speaks, the others listen. Ponyboy notices that Cherry Valance, a Soc, talks to him like a person, and that small thing changes how he sees her whole side of town.

When you read dialogue, do not just ask what was said. Ask what the speaker wanted from saying it. Ask what they left out. Ask whether their words match their actions, because a character who says "I don't care" and then checks the window every five minutes has told you something true without meaning to.

words.d: the words characters speak to each other in a story, usually shown in quotation marks
informal words used by a particular group, such as teenagers or a neighborhood

look.title: A Kitchen Argument
look.text: "You didn't call." "Phone died." "It's been dead a lot lately." "Yeah, well." Ray put the milk back in the fridge without drinking any. "Did you eat?" "I said I'm fine." Nobody had asked if he was fine.
look.prompt: What does each speaker want? What does the last line tell you about Ray that he did not intend to say?

check.q: In the brothers' example, what showed that the second brother was anxious to be forgiven?
choices: He gave a long, detailed answer ending in an apology
He spoke to a waiter sharply
check.why: The long, over-explained answer with an apology at the end shows eagerness to be forgiven.

check.q: A character says "I don't care" and then checks the window every five minutes. What should a reader conclude?
choices: The character's actions reveal the words are not true
The character is telling the truth
check.why: When words and actions disagree, the actions usually reveal the truth.

check.q: Which question is the most useful one to ask about a line of dialogue?
choices: How many words does it have?
What did the speaker want from saying it?
check.why: Asking what the speaker wanted uncovers motivation and character behind the words.

lessons.title: Static and Dynamic Characters
lessons.mainIdea: A dynamic character changes inside during the story; a static character stays the same, and both kinds have jobs to do.
reading: At the start of a story a girl believes her older cousin is perfect. By the end she has watched him lie, cover it up, and lie again, and she cannot see him the same way. She has not grown taller or changed schools. She has changed inside. A character who changes in some important way is called *dynamic*.

A character who stays the same all through the story is *static*. Static is not an insult. A story needs people who hold steady. A best friend who is loyal on page one and loyal on the last page gives the main character something to lean on. A villain who never softens gives the hero something to push against. The question is not whether a character is good or bad but whether they change.

The change in a dynamic character is usually in beliefs, values, or understanding, not in situation. A character who gets rich but thinks exactly as before is static. A character who loses everything and learns what mattered is dynamic. In The Outsiders, Ponyboy begins by seeing Socs as one thing and greasers as another. By the end he understands that people on both sides watch the same sunset. That is his change.

To track a change, find three moments: how the character sees things at the start, the event that shakes that view, and how they see things at the end. If you can name all three with evidence from the text, you can prove a character is dynamic. If the third moment matches the first, you have a static character, and you can prove that too.

words.d: a character who changes in an important way, usually in beliefs or understanding, during the story
a character who stays essentially the same from the beginning of the story to the end

look.title: Two Friends, One Summer
look.text: In June, Tasha and Rob both think the new kid, Elias, is stuck up. In July, Tasha gets stuck on a broken bus with Elias for four hours and hears about his family. In August, Tasha invites him over. Rob still calls him stuck up and does not know why Tasha bothers.
look.prompt: Which friend is dynamic and which is static? Name the event that shook the view of the one who changed.

check.q: What makes a character dynamic?
choices: Changing inside in an important way
check.why: A dynamic character changes in beliefs, values, or understanding. Action or likability is not the test.

check.q: A character wins the lottery but thinks about the world exactly as before. This character is:
choices: Dynamic, because he is rich now
Static, because his inner view did not change
Static, because he is a minor character
check.why: The change that counts is inside. A changed situation with an unchanged mind is static.

check.q: Why do stories need static characters?
choices: They give the main character something steady to lean on or push against
They always turn out to be villains
Readers prefer characters who never change
check.why: Steady characters anchor the story, as loyal friends or unchanging opponents.

lessons.title: Conflict Inside
lessons.mainIdea: Internal conflict is a struggle within one character between two things they want, fear, or believe.
reading: A boy finds a wallet with two hundred dollars in it. Nobody saw him pick it up. His family needs the money. He also knows exactly what his grandmother would say. For the next three pages he does nothing but walk and think, and those are the tensest pages in the book. Nobody is chasing him. The fight is inside.

That is *internal conflict*: a struggle within a single character. It is often written as a person versus themselves. The two sides can be a want against a value, a fear against a duty, or two loyalties that cannot both be kept. The character has to choose, and either choice costs something.

Internal conflict is what makes a character feel real rather than like a game piece. A hero who never doubts is boring. A character who wants to run and also wants to stay, who must decide and cannot, is someone you recognize. In The Outsiders, Johnny wrestles with whether to turn himself in after the park, and Ponyboy wrestles with his anger at Darry against his need for him.

You can spot internal conflict by looking for a character's thoughts that argue with each other, a decision that is put off, or a moment when a character does one thing and then undoes it. When you find one, name the two sides. "He wants the money but he wants to be honest" is a complete description of a conflict.

words.d: a struggle inside one character, such as a want fighting a value or two loyalties that cannot both be kept
a choice between two options where each one has a real cost

look.title: Three Pages of Walking
look.text: He counted it again at the corner. Two hundred and six. He thought about the electric bill on the fridge, the one with the red stamp. Then he thought about his grandmother's face, and he put the wallet in his pocket, and he took it out, and he put it back.
look.prompt: Name the two sides of this boy's conflict. What action shows that he has not decided yet?

check.q: Which of these is an internal conflict?
choices: A girl argues with her coach about playing time
A storm floods a family's basement
A boy wants to quit the team but fears letting his father down
Two friends race for the same bus
check.why: The struggle is inside one person, between a want and a fear. The others involve outside forces or other people.

check.q: Why does internal conflict make a character feel real?
choices: Real people doubt and struggle with choices too
It means the character is the narrator
It removes the need for other characters
check.why: Readers recognize inner struggle from their own lives, so a character who has it seems human.

check.q: Which clue best signals internal conflict in a text?
choices: A character doing something and then undoing it
check.why: Doing and undoing an action shows a character caught between two choices.

lessons.title: Conflict Outside
lessons.mainIdea: External conflict is a struggle between a character and something outside them: another person, society, nature, or fate.
reading: A swimmer is caught in a current. A student is called to the principal's office over a rule she thinks is unfair. Two boys in a parking lot square up over a girl. In each case the character is pushing against something outside themselves. That is *external conflict*, and most stories have more than one.

Writers and teachers usually sort external conflicts into a few kinds. Person versus person: two characters want different things. Person versus society: a character pushes against laws, customs, or what everyone expects. Person versus nature: a character fights weather, wilderness, or illness. Some add person versus fate or the supernatural, when the force is beyond human control.

The Outsiders runs on person versus society. The greasers and Socs are not just individuals who dislike each other. They are two groups that the whole town has sorted by money, and the boys inherit the fight whether they want it or not. Ponyboy's fight with the Socs at the movie theater is person versus person on the surface, but the reason those boys are enemies is the society behind them.

Internal and external conflicts usually work together. The outside fight forces the inside choice. A boy attacked in a park has an external conflict, and afterward he has an internal one: run or confess. When you describe a story's conflict, try to name one of each and show how the outside one caused the inside one.

words.d: a struggle between a character and an outside force such as another person, society, or nature
the people of a place taken as a whole, with their laws, customs, and expectations

look.title: Conflicts in One Short Model Story
look.cite: counted for this lesson from a ten-scene model story
look.prompt: This story has ten scenes. Which kind of conflict fills the most scenes? Does that tell you what the story is mostly about, or only what is loudest?

check.q: A character struggles against a rule that everyone in town accepts. Which kind of conflict is this?
check.why: The opposing force is the customs and expectations of a whole community, which is society.

check.q: In The Outsiders, why are the fights between greasers and Socs more than person versus person?
choices: Because the boys are all related
Because the whole town has sorted them into groups by money
Because the narrator makes them up
check.why: The groups exist because of the town's social divisions, so the conflict is also person versus society.

check.q: How do external and internal conflicts usually relate?
choices: The outside fight often forces an inside choice
They never appear in the same story
External conflicts only happen to villains
check.why: An outside event, like an attack, often creates an inner decision, like whether to confess.

lessons.title: First Person
lessons.mainIdea: In first-person point of view, a character tells the story as "I," so you get their thoughts but only what they know and choose to say.
reading: "I never meant to break the window." Five words in and you already have a voice, a person, and a hint that something is being explained away. The story is told by someone inside it, using I and me and my. That is *first-person point of view*. The teller is called the *narrator*.

First person gets you close. You hear the narrator's private thoughts, feel their fear, and hear the way they talk. Twain's Huckleberry Finn opens with Huck speaking straight to you in his own uneducated, honest voice, and that voice is most of why the book works. The Outsiders is first person too: everything comes through Ponyboy, including his mistakes.

But first person has walls. The narrator can only tell what they saw, heard, or were told. If Ponyboy is not in the room, you are not in the room. And a narrator can be wrong, or biased, or protecting someone. When Ponyboy says Darry does not love him, you have his feeling, not the fact. Later he learns otherwise, and so do you, but only because the book lets him find out.

When you read first person, keep two questions running. What does this narrator know? And what does this narrator want me to think? A narrator's blind spots are part of the story. Sometimes they are the whole point.

words.d: the position from which a story is told: who is telling it and how much they know
the voice that tells a story, which may be a character in it or a voice outside it
a point of view in which a character tells the story using I, me, and my

look.title: Huck Introduces Himself
look.text: You don't know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain't no matter.
look.cite: Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, 1884
look.prompt: What can you tell about Huck from this one sentence: his schooling, his attitude, how he treats the reader?

check.q: Which sentence is written in first person?
choices: She locked the door and waited.
I locked the door and waited.
He wondered whether to lock the door.
The door was locked at nine.
check.why: First person uses I, me, and my. Only the second sentence has the narrator inside the story as I.

check.q: What is a main limit of first-person point of view?
choices: The reader never learns the narrator's thoughts
The narrator must always be honest
It cannot be used in novels
The narrator can only tell what they know or were told
check.why: A first-person narrator is inside the story and cannot report scenes they did not witness.

check.q: Ponyboy says early on that Darry does not love him. How should a careful reader treat this?
choices: As a fact the author confirmed
As a clue about the setting
As the narrator's feeling, which might be wrong
check.why: A first-person narrator reports feelings and beliefs, and Ponyboy later learns he was mistaken.

lessons.title: Third Person: Limited and Omniscient
lessons.mainIdea: Third-person narrators use he, she and they; a limited narrator stays inside one character's mind, while an omniscient narrator can enter any mind.
reading: "Marisol did not hear the footsteps behind her." No character could say that about herself in the moment. The narrator is standing outside the story, using she and her, and knows something Marisol does not. That is *third-person point of view*. It comes in two main kinds, and the difference is how much the narrator can see.

A *limited* third-person narrator follows one character closely, reporting that person's thoughts and feelings but nobody else's. You see the world over that character's shoulder. It feels almost like first person, but the narrator can add things the character would not say, like "she did not hear the footsteps." Many modern novels use limited third person because it is close and clear at the same time.

An *omniscient* narrator, from a Latin word meaning all-knowing, can enter any character's mind and move from one to another, even in the same scene. Dickens often does this: he can tell you what the rich man thinks and then what the beggar at his gate thinks. Omniscient narration gives a wide view of a whole world, but it keeps you a little farther from any one person.

To tell them apart, count minds. If the narrator only ever reports one character's inner life, it is limited. If it reports two or more, it is omniscient. Then ask why the writer chose that. A mystery often stays limited so you cannot see the culprit's thoughts. A novel about a whole town goes omniscient so you can.

words.d: a point of view in which a narrator outside the story tells it using he, she, and they
third-person narration that reports the thoughts of only one character
all-knowing; third-person narration that can report the thoughts of any character

look.title: Counting Minds
look.text: Nia thought the coach had forgotten her name. The coach, watching from the bench, was thinking that Nia was the only player who never gave up, and wondering how to say so without embarrassing her.
look.prompt: How many minds does this narrator enter? Is it limited or omniscient? What do you know that Nia does not?

check.q: A narrator reports only Jamal's thoughts throughout the book, using he and him. This point of view is:
check.why: He and him make it third person, and staying inside one mind makes it limited.

check.q: What does omniscient mean?
choices: Telling the story in the past
check.why: Omniscient comes from Latin words meaning all-knowing. The narrator can enter any mind.

check.q: Why might a mystery writer choose third-person limited?
choices: So the reader cannot see the culprit's thoughts
Because it is required for mysteries
So every character's thoughts are visible
Because it uses the word I
check.why: Staying inside one mind keeps the culprit's thoughts hidden and preserves the mystery.

lessons.title: Narrators You Cannot Trust
lessons.mainIdea: An unreliable narrator tells the story in a way the reader should doubt, and the clues to that doubt are part of the story's meaning.
reading: A narrator opens by insisting he is not mad. He says his senses are sharp, that he heard things in heaven and hell, and that he will tell the story calmly to prove it. Then he explains, very calmly, how he planned a murder for a week. This is Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart," and the more the narrator insists on his sanity, the less you believe him. He is an *unreliable narrator*.

An unreliable narrator is one whose telling you cannot fully trust. Sometimes the narrator lies. More often the narrator is honest but limited: a child who does not understand what the adults are doing, a person so angry they cannot see straight, someone who wants badly to look good. The story is still true in the world of the book. The telling of it is bent.

Writers plant clues so that you can see around the narrator. Look for a gap between what the narrator claims and what other characters do or say. Look for a narrator who protests too much, like Poe's. Look for details the narrator drops without noticing what they mean. Ponyboy is mostly reliable, but he is fourteen and hurt, and when he calls Darry cold, the text shows Darry working two jobs to keep the family together.

Reading an unreliable narrator is like listening to a friend tell a story about a fight they were in. You believe the fight happened. You also know they are the hero of their own version. The skill is to hold both things at once and to keep looking for evidence.

words.d: a narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt, because of lies, limits, or bias
a leaning for or against something that shapes how a person sees and reports it

look.title: Protesting Too Much
look.text: True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?
look.prompt: The narrator has not yet told you what he did. What makes you distrust him already, in just this first sentence?

check.q: What is an unreliable narrator?
choices: A narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt
A narrator who uses third person
A narrator who never appears in the story
A narrator who tells the story out of order
check.why: Unreliable means the reader should not fully trust the telling, because of lies, limits, or bias.

check.q: Which clue most suggests a narrator is unreliable?
choices: The story is set in the past
Other characters' actions contradict what the narrator claims
check.why: A gap between the narrator's claims and what others do is a classic sign of unreliability.

check.q: Why does Poe's narrator insisting he is not mad make readers doubt him?
choices: Because sane people rarely need to insist on it so hard
Because he speaks in third person
Because the story is a comedy
check.why: Protesting too much draws attention to the very thing he denies, so readers grow suspicious.

lessons.title: Inference With Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: An inference about a character is a claim; to make it count, cite the exact words from the text that support it and explain the link.
reading: A student says, "Darry is really scared of losing his brothers." Her teacher asks, "Where?" That one word is the whole skill. In literature, what you think about a character is an *inference*, a conclusion drawn from clues. Inferences are welcome, but they have to be backed by *textual evidence*: words from the book that you can point to.

The strongest evidence is specific. "Darry acts worried" is weak. "Darry yells at Ponyboy for coming home late, then the book shows him working two jobs and turning down college" is strong, because anyone can check it. When you quote, quote only the part that matters, and put it in quotation marks. When you paraphrase, say where it comes from.

Then explain the link. Evidence does not speak for itself. Write the bridge: "Darry yells about a late night because he is responsible for keeping the family together, and one mistake could get his brothers taken away." Now a reader sees the claim, the proof, and the reasoning that connects them.

Good evidence can also prove you wrong, and that is useful. If you think a character is cruel and then find three scenes where he is kind to a stranger, your inference needs to change. Readers who go back to the text with an open mind end up knowing characters better than readers who decide early and stop looking.

words.d: a conclusion drawn from clues in the text combined with what the reader already knows
specific words or details from the text, quoted or paraphrased, that support a claim
a statement you believe is true and are prepared to support with evidence

look.title: Claim, Evidence, Link
look.text: Claim: Mr. Alvarez, the janitor in the model story, is proud of his work. Evidence: he arrives an hour before anyone else, and the narrator notices his name written neatly on every mop handle. Link: people who sign their tools care about them the way an artist cares about a painting.
look.prompt: Is the link convincing? What other evidence from a story would make the claim stronger, and what evidence would weaken it?

check.q: What is textual evidence?
choices: Specific words or details from the text that support a claim
What a friend said about the book
check.why: Textual evidence is drawn from the text itself, quoted or paraphrased, so others can check it.

check.q: Which piece of evidence is strongest for the claim 'Darry is scared of losing his brothers'?
choices: Darry works two jobs and yells when Ponyboy comes home late
check.why: Specific actions that anyone can check in the book make the strongest evidence.

check.q: After the evidence, what must a writer still add?
choices: A summary of the whole plot
The explanation linking the evidence to the claim
check.why: Evidence does not speak for itself. The reasoning that connects it to the claim completes the argument.

lessons.title: Following One Character Through a Book
lessons.mainIdea: To understand a character in a whole novel, track them at the start, at turning points, and at the end, and compare the evidence.
reading: A single scene shows you a character in one light. A whole novel shows you the same person under many lights, and the changes between them are where the meaning lives. Reading a whole book well means keeping a record, because by chapter ten you will have forgotten the exact words of chapter one.

One simple method: keep a page for each major character with three columns, labeled start, turning points, and end. Under start, write what the character wants and believes in the first chapters, with page numbers. Under turning points, note each event that pushes on those wants and beliefs. Under end, write what the character wants and believes at the close. Then compare the first and last columns.

Try it with Ponyboy in The Outsiders. At the start he believes the Socs have it easy and Darry is against him. Turning points pile up: a conversation with Cherry about sunsets, the night in the park, the days hiding in the church, the fire, the hospital, the rumble, and a note left in a book. At the end he understands that Socs have troubles too, that Darry was protecting him, and that he can tell this story instead of fighting it.

The last pages of the novel reveal that the whole book is a school assignment Ponyboy has written, and its first line is the same as the line he chooses to begin with. That structure is the author's way of saying the change is real: the boy who walked out of the theater alone is now a writer telling you why. A character sheet lets you prove that with evidence, chapter by chapter.

words.d: an event in a story that changes a character's situation, choices, or understanding
the path of change a character follows from the beginning of a story to the end

look.title: Two Brothers, Words per Line
look.cite: counted for this lesson from a short model story written for it
look.prompt: In this model story, the older brother's lines get longer and the younger brother's get shorter. What change in each character might those numbers show?

check.q: Why keep a written record of a character while reading a novel?
choices: Because readers forget the exact details of early chapters by the end
Because characters in novels never change
Because it replaces reading the book
check.why: Over hundreds of pages, memory fades. A record lets you compare early and late evidence.

check.q: What does the ending of The Outsiders reveal about the whole book?
choices: It is Ponyboy's school assignment, beginning where the book began
check.why: The last pages show Ponyboy writing the story for a class, starting with the book's own first line.

check.q: On a three-column character sheet, what belongs under turning points?
choices: Events that push on the character's wants and beliefs
check.why: Turning points are the events that change a character's situation or understanding.

review.q: 'Rosa never once looked at the clock during the three-hour exam.' This is an example of:
review.why: The sentence shows an action and lets the reader infer focus or calm. Nothing is stated outright.

review.q: A character who is loyal at the start and equally loyal at the end is best described as:
review.why: A character who does not change inside is static, whether or not the character is admirable.

review.q: Which is an example of internal conflict?
choices: A hiker lost in a blizzard
A boy who wants to tell the truth but fears losing his friend
Two sisters fighting over one bedroom
A worker who protests an unfair law
review.why: The struggle is inside one person, between a want and a fear.

review.q: In The Outsiders, the conflict between greasers and Socs is mainly:
review.why: The groups are made by the town's divisions of money and class, so the conflict is social.

review.q: A narrator uses 'she' and reports the thoughts of every character in the room. This is:
review.why: Third person with access to all minds is omniscient.

review.q: What is the best sign that a narrator is unreliable?
choices: What other characters do contradicts what the narrator claims
The story has a sad ending
review.why: A gap between the narrator's claims and the evidence in the text signals unreliability.

review.q: Which is the strongest textual evidence that a character is generous?
choices: The narrator says she seems nice
She gives her only coat to a stranger on page 42
review.why: A specific, checkable action from the text is the strongest evidence.

review.q: What is the main reason to track a character across a whole novel instead of judging from one scene?
choices: Because one scene shows one light and the changes between scenes carry the meaning
Because tests ask about chapter one
review.why: Change over the whole book is where a character's arc and the story's meaning appear.

chapters.title: Plot, Setting and Theme
chapters.bigQuestion: How does a story about particular people in a particular place end up saying something true about everyone?

story.title: The Argument About the Sunset
story.kicker: Two readers, one novel, one sunset, and a disagreement that turned out to be the whole point of the book.
paragraphs: Two eighth graders in a Chicago classroom were arguing, quietly, because the teacher was nearby. They had both finished The Outsiders. Jada said the book was about a gang fight and some boys who ran away. Miguel said it was about the sunset. Jada laughed at him. "A sunset is a sunset," she said. "He looks at the sky. It's a nice sky. Move on."

Miguel opened the book to the scene where Ponyboy, a poor greaser, talks with Cherry Valance, a rich Soc, outside a drive-in. Ponyboy tells her he watches sunsets. Cherry says she watches them too, from her side of town. Miguel pointed at the page. "Same sunset. Different sides of town. The whole book is right there." Jada read it twice and did not say anything for a while.

Then she went looking. She found the sunset again near the end, in the note Johnny leaves for Ponyboy, where he talks about staying gold and about how Ponyboy can still see sunsets like a kid does. She found a poem in the middle of the book, by Robert Frost, about how the first green of spring is gold and does not last. She found that every time the sunset came back, somebody had lost something.

By the end of the period, Jada had changed her mind, but not all the way. "Fine," she said. "The sunset means something. But the book is still about the fight. The fight is what happens. The sunset is what it means." Miguel thought about that and decided she was right. They had discovered, without the words for it yet, the difference between plot and theme.

This chapter gives you those words. Plot is what happens, in what order, and why one thing leads to the next. Setting is where and when it happens, and why the where matters. Theme is what the story says about people, the part that stays true when you close the book. Symbols, like a sunset, are how a writer gets from one to the other without preaching. You will learn to find all of them and to prove what you find.
story.think: Jada said the fight is what happens and the sunset is what it means. Can a story have what happens without what it means? Can it have meaning without events?

lessons.title: Five Parts of a Plot
lessons.mainIdea: Most plots move through exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution, and naming those parts helps you see how a story is built.
reading: A girl moves to a new town and knows nobody. She joins the track team and gets faster. A rival on the team starts sabotaging her. On the day of the championship, she has to decide whether to run or to report the rival and miss the race. She runs, and wins, and reports the rival afterward. In the last scene she is eating pizza with three new friends. You just read a whole plot, and it has five parts.

The *exposition* sets things up: who, where, and what is normal. The girl is new and alone. The *rising action* is the chain of events that builds tension: the team, the speed, the sabotage. Each event makes the next one more likely, and the stakes go up. The *climax* is the moment of highest tension, where the main character faces the central choice or conflict head on: run or report.

The *falling action* shows the results of the climax playing out: she wins and reports. The *resolution* shows the new normal: pizza with friends. Some stories skip or shrink a part. A short story might have one line of exposition. A mystery might put the climax on the last page and give you almost no falling action. But the shape is there under most stories, and once you see it, you can predict where a book is headed.

In The Outsiders, the exposition is Ponyboy's walk home and the fight, plus what he tells you about his brothers and friends. The rising action runs from the drive-in through the park. The night in the park, and the flight to the church, push the story toward its climax. Readers argue about exactly which scene is the climax, the fire or the rumble or the hospital, and that argument is a good one to have with evidence.

words.d: the opening part of a plot that introduces characters, setting, and the normal situation
the series of events that build tension toward the climax
the turning point of highest tension, where the main conflict comes to a head
the events after the climax that show its results
the ending, where conflicts are settled and a new normal is shown

look.title: Sentences per Plot Part
look.cite: counted for this lesson from the track story in the first paragraph
look.prompt: In this tiny story, the rising action gets the most sentences. In a full novel, which part usually takes the most pages, and why?

check.q: Which part of the plot introduces the characters and the normal situation?
check.why: Exposition sets up who, where, and what is normal before the tension builds.

check.q: In the track story, which event is the climax?
choices: The girl moves to a new town
The girl must decide whether to run or report the rival
The girl eats pizza with friends
The girl joins the track team
check.why: The climax is the moment of highest tension where the main choice must be made.

check.q: What is the job of rising action?
choices: To show the new normal at the end
To build tension through a chain of events that raise the stakes
check.why: Rising action is the chain of events that increases tension toward the climax.

lessons.title: Why the Climax Comes Late
lessons.mainIdea: Writers place the climax near the end and build to it so that the resolution feels earned, and the placement shapes how a reader feels.
reading: Imagine a story where the big fight happens in chapter two and the next twelve chapters are cleanup. You would put it down. Now imagine the fight comes in chapter thirteen of fourteen, after every chapter has made it harder to avoid. You cannot put it down. Same fight. Different place. Where a writer puts the *climax* controls how a reader feels for the whole book.

The rising action is supposed to make the climax feel necessary. Each event should close off an easier choice. In The Outsiders, the greasers and Socs could have kept their distance. Then a fight in a park goes wrong, and hiding becomes impossible, and a church fire turns the boys into something the town has to look at. By the time of the rumble, nobody can back out. That is the feeling of rising action done well: the walls closing in.

After the climax, the falling action and resolution are usually short, but they are not filler. They tell you what the climax cost and what it changed. A story that ends the moment the fight ends leaves you hanging. A story that shows the day after, quietly, tells you what the fight was for. The last chapters of The Outsiders are mostly Ponyboy trying to get up in the morning, and that is the point.

When you read, mark the page where you think the climax is. Then check it two ways. Was everything before it building pressure? Is everything after it release? If yes, you found it. If the pressure keeps building after your mark, you were early. Being early is not a mistake. It means the writer fooled you on purpose, and that is worth noticing too.

words.d: what a character stands to win or lose; higher stakes mean more tension
the feeling of worry or suspense a reader has while waiting to see what happens

look.title: Two Versions of One Story
look.text: Version A: Chapter 1, the twins find the map. Chapter 2, they find the treasure. Chapters 3 through 10, they spend it. Version B: Chapters 1 through 9, the twins search, lose the map, fight, and get it back. Chapter 10, they dig.
look.prompt: Which version would you rather read, and what does your answer tell you about where a climax belongs?

check.q: Why do writers usually place the climax near the end?
choices: So the tension has time to build and the ending feels earned
So the reader can skip to it
Because the climax is the least important part
check.why: A late climax gives the rising action room to close off easy choices and raise the stakes.

check.q: What should the events of rising action do to the main character's choices?
choices: Close off easier options until the conflict must be faced
check.why: Good rising action removes escape routes so the climax feels necessary.

check.q: What do the falling action and resolution tell a reader?
choices: What the climax cost and what it changed
check.why: The ending shows the results and meaning of the climax rather than just stopping.

lessons.title: Subplots
lessons.mainIdea: A subplot is a smaller story running beside the main one, and it usually reflects or pushes the main plot.
reading: The main story is about a boy trying to get his family through a hard year. Beside it, in a few scenes a chapter, is a smaller story about his sister learning to drive. The driving lessons never become the main event. But they show the same family under less pressure, and the day she finally passes her test is the day the boy first believes things might turn out. The small story is a *subplot*.

A subplot is a second, smaller plot woven through the main one. It has its own beginning, rise, and end. Writers use subplots for several reasons. A subplot can give the reader a break from the main tension. It can develop a minor character. Most importantly, it can echo the main plot's theme from a different angle, or cross into the main plot and change it.

In The Outsiders, the friendship between Ponyboy and Cherry Valance is a subplot. It does not drive the fights. But every time it appears, it shows that a greaser and a Soc can talk like people, which is what the main plot keeps saying is impossible. Sodapop's troubles with his girlfriend are another subplot, and they come crashing into the main story when Ponyboy and Darry's arguing finally becomes too much for him.

To find a subplot, look for a thread of scenes about a different problem than the main one, with its own little arc. Then ask what it is doing there. If it echoes the main plot, name the echo. If it crosses into the main plot, mark the crossing. A subplot that does neither may just be padding, and readers are allowed to say so.

words.d: a smaller story that runs alongside the main plot and usually reflects or affects it
a series of connected scenes about one problem or relationship running through a book

look.title: Spotting the Echo
look.text: Main plot: Kenji is trying to save a failing community garden before the city sells the lot. Subplot: Kenji's grandfather, who has stopped speaking since Grandma died, starts coming to the garden and, one morning, tells Kenji the name of a tomato plant.
look.prompt: How does the grandfather subplot echo the main plot? What might happen if the two threads cross?

check.q: What is a subplot?
choices: The climax of the main plot
A smaller story that runs beside the main plot
check.why: A subplot is a second, smaller story with its own arc that runs alongside the main plot.

check.q: In The Outsiders, what does the Ponyboy and Cherry subplot show?
choices: That a greaser and a Soc can talk like people
That the rumble was Cherry's idea
check.why: Their friendship echoes the theme that the two groups are not as different as the town believes.

check.q: Which is a fair test of whether a subplot belongs in a book?
choices: Whether it is longer than the main plot
Whether it has a happy ending
Whether it is about the narrator
Whether it echoes the main plot or crosses into it
check.why: A good subplot reflects or affects the main story. One that does neither may be padding.

lessons.title: Flashback and Foreshadowing
lessons.mainIdea: Flashback jumps backward to show earlier events; foreshadowing plants hints about events to come.
reading: Halfway through a scene at a funeral, the narrator says, "The last time I saw her laugh was the summer we painted the fence," and suddenly you are at the fence, three years earlier, paint on your hands. Then you are back at the funeral. The story jumped in time. That jump is a *flashback*, and it lets a writer show the past instead of just summarizing it.

Writers use flashback when the past explains the present. A character's fear of water makes sense once you see the day at the lake. The clue that the story is jumping is usually a change of verb tense, a line like "years before," or a sense memory that pulls the narrator back. When you notice one, ask what the writer needs you to see now that you could not have understood earlier.

*Foreshadowing* works the other way. It plants a hint about something that has not happened yet. A character mentions that the old bridge is unsafe. Nobody crosses it for a hundred pages. When someone finally does, you feel a chill because you were warned. Foreshadowing can be a line of dialogue, an object, a bit of weather, or even a title. It is often only visible the second time you read.

In The Outsiders, Ponyboy's early remark that he wishes he looked tougher foreshadows how much his looks and his innocence will matter. Johnny's carrying a knife after he was beaten foreshadows the park. On a first read, these are details. On a second read, they are the writer telling you exactly what is coming, if you are paying attention.

words.d: a scene that interrupts the story to show something that happened earlier
a hint or clue placed early in a story about something that will happen later
the form of a verb that shows when something happens, such as past or present

look.title: A Hint in the First Paragraph
look.text: The ice on the pond was thick enough, everyone said, if you stayed near the edge. Tomas nodded and did not mention that the middle was where the fish were.
look.prompt: What is being foreshadowed? Which words do the work? How would you feel if Tomas appeared with a fishing pole in chapter four?

check.q: A scene interrupts the present action to show what happened three years earlier. This is:
check.why: A jump backward in time to show an earlier event is a flashback.

check.q: Why do writers use flashback rather than just summarizing the past?
choices: It lets readers see the past scene and feel it, not just hear about it
It hides the past from the reader
check.why: Showing a scene gives readers the experience, which is stronger than a summary.

check.q: Which is the best example of foreshadowing?
choices: A character remembers her first day of school
The narrator explains the town's history
A character says the old bridge is unsafe, and much later someone crosses it
check.why: An early hint that pays off later is foreshadowing.

lessons.title: Setting That Does Work
lessons.mainIdea: Setting is when and where a story happens, and in good writing it shapes characters, creates conflict, and builds mood.
reading: Take a story about two friends who fall out and set it in a Chicago apartment in January, with the radiators clanking and nobody able to go outside. Now set the same story in a wide, empty field in June. The words the friends say could be identical, but the stories are not. In the first, they are trapped together. In the second, one can walk away. The *setting* changed what the fight can be.

Setting is the time and place of a story: the year, the season, the hour, the city, the room. Weak writing treats it as a backdrop, a painted wall behind the actors. Strong writing makes it do work. Setting can shape characters, because a boy raised in a town that sorts people by money grows up thinking that is normal. Setting can create conflict, because a blizzard or a border or a curfew is a force to fight against.

Setting also builds *mood*, the feeling a reader gets from a scene. A writer chooses details on purpose: a dripping faucet, a streetlight buzzing, a hallway that smells like floor cleaner. Each one tunes the reader's nerves. When you notice a writer spending a paragraph on a place, ask what feeling the details are building and what that feeling is for.

The Outsiders never names its city, but its setting is precise: a mid-1960s American town with an east side and a west side, drive-in theaters, vacant lots for fights, and an abandoned church in the countryside. The east-west line is the whole conflict. The church, far from town, is the one place a greaser and a Soc could not be told apart, which is exactly what the boys learn there.

words.d: the time and place in which a story happens, including season, hour, and specific locations
the feeling a piece of writing creates in the reader, such as dread, calm, or loneliness

look.title: Same Fight, Two Rooms
look.text: A: The radiator knocked twice and went silent. Snow leaned against the window. Dee sat on the far end of the couch, which was not very far. B: The field ran to the tree line. Dee stood up, brushed off her jeans, and could have been a mile away in a minute.
look.prompt: Which details build mood in each version? In which version is the coming argument more dangerous, and why?

check.q: What is setting?
choices: The main conflict of a story
The time and place in which a story happens
check.why: Setting is the when and where, from the era down to the specific room.

check.q: In the two-friends example, how did setting change the story?
choices: It changed whether the friends were trapped together or free to leave
check.why: The winter apartment traps them; the open field lets one walk away. Setting changed the conflict.

check.q: Why does the abandoned church matter as a setting in The Outsiders?
choices: It is far from the town's east-west divide, so the boys are not sorted there
It is where the rumble happens
It is on the west side
check.why: Away from town, the social line disappears, which lets the boys see themselves differently.

lessons.title: Theme, Topic and Moral
lessons.mainIdea: A topic is what a story is about in a word; a theme is what it says about that topic in a sentence; a moral is a lesson it orders you to follow.
reading: Ask three students what The Outsiders is about. One says "friendship." One says "people on both sides of a divide have the same fears and the same sky." One says "don't judge people by their money." All three are pointing at something real, but they are pointing at three different things: a topic, a theme, and a moral.

A *topic* is a subject, usually one or two words: friendship, class, loss, growing up. A topic is not yet an idea. A *theme* is what the story says about the topic, and it takes a full sentence: "Loyalty to friends can cost more than it gives." A theme is an insight about people or life that the story shows to be true, and a strong novel has more than one.

A *moral* is a direct lesson or rule, the kind that ends a fable: be honest, work hard, do not judge. Fables have morals. Most novels do not. A novel with a moral tends to feel like a lecture. A novel with a theme trusts you to think. The difference is that a theme describes how the world is, and a moral tells you what to do about it.

When you write a theme, avoid two mistakes. Do not stop at the topic: "The book is about class" is a start, not a theme. Do not name the characters: "Ponyboy learns that Socs have problems too" is a plot summary. A theme leaves the characters behind and says something that could be true outside the book: "People who seem to have everything can still be hurting."

words.d: the subject of a story in a word or two, such as friendship or loss
an insight about people or life that a story shows to be true, stated as a full sentence
a direct lesson or rule that a story teaches, common in fables

look.title: Sort the Three
look.text: About one short story, three readers wrote: (1) Courage. (2) Always stand up to bullies. (3) Being brave often means being scared and acting anyway. One is a topic, one is a moral, one is a theme.
look.prompt: Which is which? Rewrite the moral as a theme, and turn the topic into a theme of your own.

check.q: Which of these is a theme rather than a topic or a moral?
choices: Family can be the people who choose to stay, not only the people you are born to
check.why: A theme is a full-sentence insight about life that reaches beyond the characters.

check.q: What is the difference between a theme and a moral?
choices: A theme describes how the world is; a moral tells you what to do
A moral is only found in novels
check.why: Themes are insights; morals are instructions. Fables have morals; most novels have themes.

check.q: Why is 'Ponyboy learns that Socs have problems too' not a good theme statement?
choices: It names the characters, so it is plot summary rather than an idea about life
check.why: A theme should be true outside the book, so it should not depend on the characters' names.

lessons.title: How a Theme Grows
lessons.mainIdea: Theme is not stated once; it develops across a whole text through repeated situations, changing characters, and the ending.
reading: A theme is not hiding in one sentence you can underline. It grows. Early in a book a situation comes up. Later it comes up again, a little different. A character reacts one way the first time and another way the last time. The ending tips the balance. By the last page, the book has made an argument without ever stating it, and you have to put it into words yourself.

The best way to watch a theme grow is to follow one *pattern*: a repeated situation, image, or question. In The Outsiders, the pattern is people looking at each other across a line. Greasers look at Socs and see money. Socs look at greasers and see trouble. Then Cherry talks to Ponyboy. Then a Soc named Randy tells Ponyboy he is tired of the fighting. Each time the pattern returns, the line gets a little thinner.

Character change is the second way theme develops. When a *dynamic* character ends up believing something new, the book is usually asking you to consider believing it too. Ponyboy's shift from "they have it easy" to "things are rough all over" is the theme walking on two legs. If you can describe the change, you can state the theme.

The ending is the last word. A story that ends with a reunion says something different from one that ends with a funeral, even if everything before was the same. When you write about theme, use all three sources: the pattern, the change, and the ending. A theme with evidence from all three is hard to argue with.

words.d: a situation, image, or question that repeats through a text, often carrying its theme
to grow and become clearer over time, as a theme does across a whole text

look.title: One Pattern Across a Model Story
look.cite: counted for this lesson from a nine-chapter model story written for it
look.prompt: The pattern peaks in chapter 7 and nearly vanishes in chapter 9. What might have happened in the story to make crossing the line stop mattering?

check.q: Which is the best description of how theme works in a novel?
choices: It is stated in one sentence in chapter one
It develops across the text through patterns, character change, and the ending
It is the same as the plot
It is only found in the title
check.why: Theme grows through repeated situations, changing characters, and how things end.

check.q: In The Outsiders, what repeated pattern carries the theme?
choices: Characters looking at each other across a social line
check.why: The book keeps returning to greasers and Socs seeing each other, and the line thins each time.

check.q: Two stories are identical except one ends with a reunion and one with a funeral. What is true?
choices: The endings give them different themes
check.why: The ending is the last word on what a story says, so different endings mean different themes.

lessons.title: Symbols and Motifs
lessons.mainIdea: A symbol is a thing in a story that stands for a larger idea; a motif is a repeated element that builds meaning; both need evidence, not guesswork.
reading: A sunset is light hitting the atmosphere at a low angle. In The Outsiders it is also the one thing a greaser and a Soc can share, and a sign of the innocence Johnny begs Ponyboy to keep. When a concrete thing in a story carries a larger meaning, it is a *symbol*. The sunset does not stop being a sunset. It becomes a sunset and something more.

Writers signal symbols by repetition and by placement. A thing that appears once is probably just a thing. A thing that appears at the beginning, at a turning point, and at the end, and that characters talk about, is asking to be read. The gold in Frost's poem, which Ponyboy recites in the church, links up with the sunset and with Johnny's last words, and together they make one symbol out of three pieces.

A *motif* is a repeated element, like an image, a phrase, or a sound, that builds meaning over a text. Motifs are broader than symbols. In The Outsiders, hair is a motif: the greasers' long hair is their pride and their label, and cutting it in the church is a real loss. A motif may not stand for one idea the way a symbol does, but it keeps a theme in front of you.

Be careful. Not everything means something, and readers who insist that every blue curtain stands for sadness get things wrong. Test a symbol the way you test any inference: find the repetitions, find the placement, find a character or narrator who treats it as important, and state what it stands for in the book's own terms. If you cannot find that evidence, it is a curtain.

words.d: a concrete thing in a story that also stands for a larger idea
an image, phrase, or element that repeats through a text and builds meaning
the state of not yet knowing the world's harm; freshness of seeing

look.title: The Poem in the Church
look.text: Nature's first green is gold, / Her hardest hue to hold.
look.cite: Robert Frost, "Nothing Gold Can Stay," 1923 (the poem Ponyboy recites in The Outsiders)
look.prompt: Gold here is not metal. What is it? How does the poem's idea of gold connect to the sunset and to Johnny's note?

check.q: What is a symbol in literature?
choices: A word that is spelled with capital letters
A concrete thing that also stands for a larger idea
check.why: A symbol is a real object, place, or image in the story that carries added meaning.

check.q: What is the best evidence that something in a story is a symbol?
choices: It repeats at key moments and characters treat it as important
check.why: Repetition, placement at turning points, and characters' attention signal a symbol.

check.q: How does a motif differ from a symbol?
choices: A motif is a repeated element that builds meaning; a symbol stands for a specific larger idea
A motif is always a color
check.why: Motifs repeat and keep a theme in view; symbols stand for something specific.

lessons.title: The Book and the Movie
lessons.mainIdea: Comparing a novel to its film shows what each form can and cannot do, and every change a filmmaker makes is a choice worth explaining.
reading: In 1983 the director Francis Ford Coppola made The Outsiders into a movie with a cast of young actors who later became famous. Students who read the book and then watch the film usually notice the same things. The movie looks right: the hair, the cars, the lot. But something is missing. Ponyboy's thoughts, which fill every page, are mostly gone, because a camera cannot film a thought.

That is the first thing a comparison teaches: the two forms have different tools. A novel can go inside a mind. It can stretch a moment across three pages or skip a year in a sentence. A film has faces, music, light, and sound, and it can make you feel a sunset in one shot that took the book a paragraph. Neither is better. Each has to do the other's work in its own way.

The second thing to learn is that every change is a choice. Filmmakers cut scenes for time, add scenes for clarity, and move things around for pace. When you notice a difference, do not just say the movie left it out. Ask what the change does. Does it make a character simpler? Does it lose a subplot that carried a theme? Does it make the ending happier or sadder than the book's? The original release of The Outsiders film trimmed the story's beginning and end, and a later, longer edition restored some of those scenes.

To write a comparison, pick one scene that both versions include. Describe exactly what each does with it. Then argue which version served the theme better and why. That is a fair fight, and it teaches you more about the book than praising or bashing the movie ever could.

words.d: a work changed from one form to another, such as a novel made into a film
the speed at which a story moves; films and books control it with different tools

look.title: What the Camera Cannot Do
look.text: In the novel, Ponyboy spends a paragraph after the fight describing how tough he wishes he looked, how he feels about his brothers, and why he does not like to be touched. In the film, the same moment is a boy on the sidewalk with a cut on his face, and the camera holds on him for three seconds.
look.prompt: What did the film lose and what did it gain? What could an actor do in three seconds to carry some of what the paragraph said?

check.q: Why do readers of The Outsiders often feel something is missing from the film?
choices: The film changes the setting to a big city
Ponyboy's inner thoughts, which fill the book, cannot be filmed directly
check.why: A novel goes inside a mind; a camera shows only what can be seen and heard.

check.q: What is the most useful question to ask about a difference between a book and its film?
choices: What does the change do to characters or theme?
check.why: Every change is a choice, and the effect of the change is what matters in a comparison.

check.q: Which is a fair method for writing a book-versus-film comparison?
choices: Listing every scene the film cut
Saying which one you liked more
Choosing one shared scene and arguing which version served the theme better
check.why: A focused, evidence-based comparison of one scene teaches more than a list or a preference.

lessons.title: Writing About Theme
lessons.mainIdea: A strong theme paragraph states the theme as a sentence, supports it with specific evidence from the text, and explains how the evidence shows the theme.
reading: Here is a weak paragraph about theme: "The theme of The Outsiders is that people are the same. Ponyboy learns this. It is a good lesson." It names a topic, not a theme. It has no evidence. It ends with an opinion. A teacher reading it cannot tell whether the writer read the book. Here is how to fix it, step by step.

First, state the theme as a full sentence about life, not about the characters: "People divided by money and class often share the same fears and the same losses." Second, give specific evidence from the text. Not "Cherry and Ponyboy talk," but the sunset exchange at the drive-in, where Cherry says she watches the same sunset from her side of town. Add a second piece: Randy, a Soc, telling Ponyboy he is sick of the fighting.

Third, explain the link. "Both moments show a Soc admitting to a greaser something the town says they cannot share. The sunset is the same sky over both neighborhoods, and Randy's exhaustion is the same fear both sides feel. The book puts these scenes at its center to show that the line between the groups is drawn by money, not by what people actually feel."

Finally, deal with the other side. A strong paragraph admits what might argue against the theme, such as the fact that the fighting does not stop, and answers it: the book does not claim the line disappears, only that it is not real in the way the boys believed. Claim, evidence, reasoning, and an honest look at the other side. That is a paragraph a teacher can trust.

words.d: the explanation that connects evidence to a claim and shows why the evidence proves it
a point that seems to argue against your claim, which a strong writer names and answers

look.title: A Theme Paragraph, Marked
look.text: CLAIM: Loyalty can ask more of a person than fairness would. EVIDENCE: In the model story, Ana lies to the principal to protect her brother even though she knows he broke the window. REASONING: She chooses her brother over the truth and pays for it with a suspension, which shows the cost the story is weighing. OTHER SIDE: Some readers say she was just afraid. But she says herself that she would do it again.
look.prompt: Find the four parts. Which part would you cut if you had to, and what would the paragraph lose?

check.q: What is wrong with 'The theme of The Outsiders is that people are the same'?
choices: It is a topic-like statement with no evidence or reasoning
check.why: It is vague, has no support from the text, and does not explain anything.

check.q: In a theme paragraph, what is the job of reasoning?
choices: To explain how the evidence shows the theme
check.why: Reasoning is the bridge between the evidence and the claim.

check.q: Why should a theme paragraph mention the other side?
choices: Because it makes the paragraph longer
Because teachers require exactly four parts
Because it proves the theme is wrong
Because answering a fair objection makes the claim more trustworthy
check.why: Naming and answering a counterargument shows you have thought honestly about the text.

review.q: Which part of a plot shows the results of the climax playing out?
review.why: Falling action follows the climax and shows what it caused.

review.q: Why does a late climax usually make a story better?
choices: It gives tension time to build so the ending feels earned
It removes the need for a resolution
It lets readers skip the middle
review.why: Rising action needs room to close off easy choices and raise the stakes.

review.q: A story pauses to show what a character saw at the lake years earlier. This is:
review.why: A scene that jumps back in time to show an earlier event is a flashback.

review.q: Which is the best example of setting doing real work in a story?
choices: A story mentions it is Tuesday
A blizzard traps two enemies in one cabin so they must deal with each other
A character wears a red shirt
review.why: The setting creates the conflict by forcing the characters together.

review.q: Which statement is a theme, not a topic or a moral?
choices: Losing someone can teach a person what they still have
review.why: It is a full-sentence insight about life that does not depend on character names.

review.q: How does a theme develop over a whole novel?
choices: It is stated in the first sentence
Through repeated patterns, character change, and the ending
It does not; only fables have themes
review.why: Theme grows across the text and is confirmed by how the story ends.

review.q: What separates a symbol from an ordinary object in a story?
choices: Symbols are named in the title
Symbols repeat at key moments and stand for a larger idea, supported by evidence
review.why: A symbol must earn its meaning through repetition, placement, and characters' attention.

review.q: A film leaves out a novel's narrator's thoughts. What is the best way to discuss this?
choices: Explain what the change does to character and theme, and how the film tries to make up for it
Say the book is too long
Ignore it because films cannot show thoughts
review.why: A good comparison treats each change as a choice with effects, not as a mistake.

chapters.title: Reading a Whole Book
chapters.bigQuestion: What do strong readers actually do, page by page, that makes a whole book theirs?

story.title: The Story That Told You Its Ending First
story.kicker: A three-page story from 1894, read once for the shock and once more for the clues, changed how one reader reads everything.
paragraphs: Andre read Kate Chopin's "The Story of an Hour" in one sitting on the bus, because it is only about a thousand words long. A woman named Mrs. Mallard is told, gently, that her husband has died in a train accident. She weeps, goes to her room alone, and sits by an open window. Then something strange happens. Instead of grief, she feels a rising joy. She whispers a word to herself: free. She had loved him, sometimes. But now the years ahead belong to her.

Then the front door opens and her husband walks in. He was nowhere near the accident. The story ends with one sentence: the doctors said she died of heart disease, of the joy that kills. Andre sat back. He had not seen it coming. He thought the ending was a trick, a twist thrown in to shock the reader. He said so in class the next day, and his teacher asked him to read it again, out loud, slowly, starting with the first sentence.

The first sentence says that Mrs. Mallard has a heart trouble, and that is why the news was broken to her gently. Andre stopped. He had read that sentence yesterday and skipped right over it. He kept going. The story is built on that heart. Her sister worries she will make herself ill. The joy she feels is described as something that runs through her body, that she cannot beat back. The ending was in the first line. The writer had told him, and he had not been listening.
